items.title: Microsoft Struggles to Repair Worldwide Outage. Here's What You Need to Know
items.standfirst: The outage impacting various Microsoft 365 services has caused disruption to governments and businesses globally. Here's what you need to know.
items.content: The icons for a range of Microsoft apps, including Microsoft Outlook, seen on a laptop, in London, England, on Nov. 13, 2026. —Yui Mok—Getty ImagesAn outage affecting Microsoft services including Outlook, Teams, and Copilot has stretched into a second day, leaving businesses and governments around the world struggling to access email communications.As of Friday midday ET, almost 24 hours since the outage was first reported, Microsoft said it was observing "signs of sustained recovery" across its services, with email queues "approaching normal levels." Full recovery efforts continued.The company reported "no evidence of malicious activity associated with the incident" at this time. "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," Microsoft said in an update. "We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions."Outlook and Teams are widely-used workplace applications, with hundreds of millions of users. The disruption to the services has left some affected workers unable to access their emails, host meetings, or complete other Microsoft-dependent office tasks.Governments and companies impacted worldwideMunicipal governments across the United States are still encountering significant system issues, with digital communications interrupted.Baltimore County Government said its staff are "currently unable to send or receive emails due to the widespread Microsoft outage,” but assured the public that 911 and other essential county services had not been affected. The City of Jacksonville, Florida, and City of Austin, Texas, reported similar disruptions to its email capabilities. Tech businesses have also faced disruptions to their day-to-day operations.Users of two leading artificial intelligence companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, reported failures involving Microsoft 365 integration tools.Overseas, the U.K. government said it is still “experiencing problems sending and receiving emails.” The outage also impacted Britain’s National Health Service (NHS), raising concerns about access to appointments and hospital schedules. Some NHS practices have reported not being able to send or receive emails, while others are still assessing the overall impact of the outage. Patients have been advised to make contact via phone rather than using email. As a result, some NHS boards have warned of an increased demand across phone lines.In Japan, lawmaker Masanao Ozaki said the outage had affected the government's IT infrastructure and that officials were “closely watching the company's response.” Meanwhile, the Philippines' Supreme Court warned that “responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed.”In India, the outage disrupted operations at several airlines, with IndiGo and Akasa Air reporting problems related to its customer-support email services.In Australia, federal bodies including intelligence agency ASIO and the Australian Federal Police were affected. Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke reiterated that Microsoft did not believe it was dealing with a cyberattack, suggesting the disruption could instead be related to a faulty software update."They believe they are dealing in some ways similar ‌to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike, where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke said at a press conference.A major Microsoft IT outage in 2024 grounded flights, sent TV stations off air, and disrupted online hospital systems. The malfunction was linked to a third party, a cybersecurity technology firm named CrowdStrike. The current Microsoft outage began Thursday and peaked in the afternoon, with outage-tracking website Downdetector.com recording nearly 130,000 reports of Outlook problems and more than 45,000 reports involving Microsoft 365 in the U.S. around 1 p.m. E.T.How Microsoft is responding Microsoft has continued to issue updates as its engineers work to restore affected services. The company said it would restart and repair impacted infrastructure, before gradually bringing the services back online.Engineers were also exploring additional measures, such as actively restarting and validating affected servers and using automated recovery systems to find and restart unresponsive servers, in an effort to speed up the process.TIME has reached out to Microsoft for further information.This isn’t the first time Microsoft has experienced an outage. In addition to the 2024 CrowdStrike incident, the company also experienced disruptions affecting Microsoft 365 in January this year and flagged connectivity issues across multiple regions with its Azure cloud platform in October last year.A return to faxes and phonesThe Microsoft outage has prompted some offices to resort to more dated forms of technology. Traders in Japan have reported a return to analog measures, sending faxes to get deals over the line rather than using email confirmations.Ryutaro Kimura, a Tokyo-based senior bond strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management, told Bloomberg that trading itself is largely unaffected "desks were still getting trades done by phone and fax.”Companies across the country's leading industries have also urged customers to avoid email in the interim. Tokyo International Air Cargo Terminal, for example, told customers to reach out phone or fax.

items.title: Van Hollen Challenges Schumer for Senate Majority Leader
items.standfirst: The senator from Maryland answered calls from progressives for new Democratic leadership, but Schumer insists he has the votes to stay in charge of the caucus.
items.content: Chris Van Hollen will challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate Majority Leader in the new Congress, marking the first time in decades that the race will be contested.Announcing his run on Thursday evening, the Democratic senator for Maryland said his challenge was “not about any one individual” but about “answering the call of the American people.”“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies — but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement on social media. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership.”Van Hollen’s announcement comes amid calls from grassroots groups and several Democratic politicians for a shake-up in the party’s leadership. Detractors have accused Schumer of being too willing to compromise and not forceful enough in confronting President Donald Trump. Others have credited him with the Democrats’ sweeping success in the midterm elections, which saw the party win a majority in both chambers of Congress. Van Hollen, a progressive Democrat, previously said he was considering running for President in 2028. Both he and Schumer are up for re-election in 2028.Read More: The Democratic Wins No Election Forecaster ExpectedIn response to Van Hollen’s announcement, Schumer, a senator for New York who has led the Democratic caucus in the upper chamber since 2017, asserted that he has enough votes to win.“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer posted. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”Senate Democrats are due for a closed-door vote on Dec. 1 on who will be their Senate Majority Leader when the new congress convenes on Jan. 4. The last time the election for Senate Democratic leader was contested was in 1994, when Tom Daschle of South Dakota defeated Chris Dodd of Connecticut in an open race to succeed retiring leader George Mitchell.A progressive challengerVan Hollen was elected to the Senate in 2016 to succeed retiring Maryland Democrat Barbara Mikulski and was reelected for a second term in 2022. He chaired the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm during the 2018 election cycle.In his time in the senate, Van Hollen emerged as a prominent progressive voice through his criticism of U.S. military support for Israel and his opposition to the Trump Administration’s policies. He has criticized Schumer for his alignment with pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC. On Thursday, Van Hollen said the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which is currently chaired by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D, N.Y.), should not accept money from AIPAC. (The DSCC accepted a direct donation of $15,000 from AIPAC’s PAC in the 2025-26 cycle, according to trackers of Federal Election Commission filings, while Democratic House and Senate candidates this cycle received around $23.9 million through AIPAC PAC through Oct. 14, including individual donations it forwarded and its own direct contributions. AIPAC’s super PAC, United Democracy Project, also spent around $54.2 million on House and Senate races through Nov. 11, though its largest contribution was toward the campaign against Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.)Before entering the Senate, Van Hollen served seven terms in the House, representing Maryland’s 8th district. He was first elected in 2002 after defeating establishment-backed Democrat Mark Shriver in a competitive primary and Republican incumbent Connie Morella in the general election. A close ally of then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Van Hollen chaired the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee in 2008 when Barack Obama won the presidency and Democrats expanded their House majority. He also oversaw House Democrats’ campaign during the 2010 cycle, when Democrats lost control of the chamber.Van Hollen said on Thursday that he would use the Senate’s full power to push to end Trump’s war with Iran and lower the cost of living. He also joined Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Bernie Sanders of Vermont, and Tammy Duckworth of Illinois in opposing any short-term government funding package that did not restrict funding for the war.“Last week the voters sent a loud and clear message: we cannot return to business as usual in Washington. We need to meet the moment with a bold agenda to deliver for working people,” Van Hollen said in a post on X announcing his run for the leadership position, adding in another post: “To deliver, we need new leadership.”Calls for a new directionVan Hollen’s announcement answered calls from progressive activists and several Democratic senators for a challenge to party leadership.Sanders, an Independent who caucuses with Democrats, ruled out backing Schumer earlier this week.“The moment when you have more income and wealth inequality than we’ve ever had in the history of this country, when our younger generation will have a lower standard of living than their parents, the time is now to deal with the need to create an economy that works for all, not just the people on top,” Sanders said at a press conference on Tuesday. “Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction? No.”Sanders endorsed Van Hollen on Thursday, saying in a social media post that voters “want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families.”Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D, Mich.) said at the same Tuesday press conference that she would not back Schumer. She did not endorse Van Hollen, but she said they had a “really productive conversation” earlier in the week. She called for anyone seeking to lead the Senate to put out a plan for what they would do in its first 100 days.“You can’t lead people if you can’t lay out where you’re going, and it may be one thing when you’re in the minority, but it’s very different when it’s now your responsibility to deliver,” she said. “Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitely different.”Several incoming Democratic senators also called for new leadership, including Troy Jackson of Maine, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Juliana Stratton of Illinois, and Annie Andrews of South Carolina. Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom also did not commit support to Schumer, telling MS Now on Thursday, “I gotta know my options,” though he added that he did not think it was “a good thing” that the Democratic Party’s leaders in Congress, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Schumer, “both live in the same borough” of New York.Read More: The Candidates Who Made History in the MidtermsTexas Sen.-elect James Talarico declined to back Schumer till he heard his “vision” for the Senate. New Hampshire Sen.-elect Chris Pappas said in an interview last month that “voters are hungry for … a new generation of leadership in the Senate.”El-Sayed, a progressive who defeated Schumer’s preferred candidate, Rep. Haley Stevens, in Michigan’s Democratic primary, endorsed Van Hollen on Thursday night.“The American public spoke clearly last week. They rejected Trumpism,” El-Sayed said in a post. “But we have yet to earn our mandate. That will require bold leadership.”Progressive groups MoveOn, Indivisible, and the Working Families Party opposed Schumer. The organizations said they would support primary challenges against Democratic senators up for reelection in 2028 who do not back Van Hollen, the New York Times reported.“Chuck Schumer’s leadership for the last two years is part of the old era of politics that needs to be put to rest,” Indivisible said in a memo released after the midterm elections. “Everyone with a Democratic senator—including those with newly-elected senators on their way to D.C.—should be demanding a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”Several House members, who do not have a say in the Senate leadership election, signalled support for change. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D, N.Y.) said on Tuesday that calls for new leadership “are a sentiment that is seen in a lot of places.” She declined to endorse Schumer, saying the decision belonged to senators. In the House leadership contest, she said that Jeffries, whom progressives have also criticized, currently faces no challenge for Speaker.A divided caucusDespite calls for a new direction, Schumer retains substantial support among Senate Democrats, buoyed by colleagues who credit his fundraising and candidate recruitment with helping deliver their midterm victories. Democrats flipped at least eight Republican-held seats, securing a caucus of at least 55 members, including two independents, up from 47. (Alaska’s Senate race has yet to be called.)Fourteen senators and senators-elect have publicly backed Schumer: Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland; Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut; Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin; Sherrod Brown of Ohio; Catherine Cortez Masto and Jacky Rosen of Nevada; John Fetterman of Pennsylvania; Ruben Gallego and Mark Kelly of Arizona; Gillibrand of New York; Tim Kaine of Virginia; Angus King of Maine; Brian Schatz of Hawaii; and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island.“When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract. And this has been a, you know, a really good election cycle for us,” Gallego said on Tuesday.In private caucus meetings this week, Schumer outlined a broad agenda for Democrats’ first 100 days in power, the Associated Press reported. It includes legislation on tariffs and health care, as well as efforts to end the war in Iran.Schumer said on Tuesday he was “confident” he would be elected Majority Leader.Van Hollen, however, portrayed the Democratic midterm victory as a “people-powered movement,” rather than one “orchestrated” by the DSCC.Schumer also faces criticism for what some saw as a slowness to support progressive candidates during this election cycle. National Democrats faced criticism for initially investing too cautiously in Mississippi, where Colom defied pre-election forecasts to become the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the state since the Reconstruction era. Schumer also backed Stevens in the primary race against El-Sayed in Michigan, before supporting the latter after he won the nomination.Van Hollen told MS Now that the Senate Democratic leader should not take sides in primaries for open seats.Van Hollen said that he had consulted a large number of incumbent and incoming Democratic senators and believed he had “more than 10” of the 55 Democratic senators and senators-elect’s votes.“Am I the underdog? Yes,” Van Hollen said.But he argued that Schumer’s support could shift now that colleagues had another candidate to consider.“It is one thing to have someone’s support when you’re the only choice,” he said. “I think a little democracy in the Senate Democratic Caucus is a good thing.”

clusters.title: What An Early Polar Vortex Combined With El Niño Means For Winter Weather
clusters.neutral_headline: What An Early Polar Vortex Combined With El Niño Means For Winter Weather

items.title: What An Early Polar Vortex Combined With El Niño Means For Winter Weather
items.content: A record-early breakdown of the polar vortex is expected to bring cold weather to the United States by the end of the month.The expected wobble in the polar vortex that sends Arctic temperatures south, however, could be in competition with the strong El Niño forecast for this winter—but experts say that how it will impact our weather remains to be seen. What is the polar vortex?The polar vortex is a low-pressure band of air centered over the North Pole in the stratosphere, where it typically sits close to the pole and rotates cyclonically around the region. Every few winters, the polar vortex will be disrupted, causing what is known as sudden stratospheric warming, in which temperatures in the stratosphere jump by 50-70 degrees in a few days. That can displace cold air, pushing it down towards parts of North America, Europe, or Asia.A wobbly polar vortex can shape weather in the northern hemisphere—though it typically takes a few weeks for its impact to be felt. The breakdown causes cold air that is usually trapped to spill out of the Arctic toward lower latitudes, triggering a cold snap. “If the polar vortex gets disrupted and weakens, then that cold air tends tends to be released southward into the mid-latitudes, and of course, with more cold air, you can also have an increased chance or risk of snowstorms or ice storms,” says Judah Cohen, a climate scientist at MIT.The polar vortex disruption currently being observed by meteorologists is the earliest ever recorded, as it typically weakens during the second half of winter. “Typically we think of this happening toward the end of the winter, in January or February,” says Andrew Charlton-Perez, professor of meteorology at the University of Reading. “So what's unusual about this event is that it's the earliest recorded sudden warming event.” How will the polar vortex interact with El Niño? The polar vortex is expected to bring chilly temperatures to the U.S. by Thanksgiving week. However, what happens beyond that is still uncertain. A weak polar vortex in November by no means dictates the rest of the winter. “This is not going to determine how our winter is going to be,” says Cohen. “It could make it colder right at the start of winter, but I don't think its influence will last much longer than that.”Experts say that it’s too early to say how the so-called “super El Niño” might interact with the polar vortex. “Because these events are so rare, we have perhaps 45 or so of these events that we've ever observed,” says Charlton-Perez. El Niño years typically bring milder temperatures, but much depends on how it interacts with the polar vortex over the rest of the winter. There’s a chance El Niño and the polar vortex work together, which would mean this winter would have mild weather in store. “If the pole vortex is in a strong circular state [for the rest of winter], then it's going to influence our weather to be mild, and the El Niño influences our weather to be mild, so they're reinforcing each other,” says Cohen. However, if the El Niño and polar vortex work against each other, what the weather looks like could just depend on which force wins out. “If the polar vortex weakens and wobbles and meanders around the northern hemisphere, then the polar vortex is really favoring [colder weather] so then it'll be a battle,” Cohen adds.Just how it all plays out remains to be seen. “We've never had a polar vortex disruption of this magnitude and a super El Nino,” says Cohen. “So in some ways, this is uncharted territory.”

items.title: Trump Envoys Witkoff and Kushner Meet With Putin in Moscow for Ukraine Talks
items.standfirst: The U.S. envoys are set to meet later with Zelensky, who has reported further disruptions to Ukraine's Starshield service.
items.content: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow Thursday to discuss Ukraine, after two days of U.S.-led talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi yielded no major breakthroughs.“I think progress was made. I think it was made earlier today,” Witkoff told reporters after the meeting at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin. “People didn't think that we were going to restart trilateral. We’ve restarted it. We’ve set a new meeting. This is what President [Donald] Trump wants to see."He went on to say that a European representative would be present for the next stage of the talks, which are set to look at the continent’s wider security arrangements. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he said.Witkoff and Kushner are now en route to Dublin, where they are set to brief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on any developments from the talks. Zelensky is among the dozens of world leaders in the Irish capital for the European Political Community summit.Zelensky has expressed optimism about the next round of negotiations, saying there is a "window of opportunity” to reach a peace deal with Russia.“There really is this window of opportunity, when all the participants involved in this negotiating process could get the result by the beginning of 2027,” he said, speaking alongside Irish Taoiseach (Prime Minister) Micheál Martin during a press conference in Dublin.Russia and Ukraine remain divided on key issuesAlthough Russian and Ukrainian negotiators ⁠reported some progress during this week's Abu Dhabi talks—including a prisoner swap agreement—all sides have acknowledged that significant differences remain, particularly over territory.Kyiv has strongly rejected Putin's demands to surrender the entirety of the eastern Donbas. With negotiations over territory deadlocked, U.S. mediators instead sought to steer discussions toward post-war security guarantees and reconstruction.However, Putin doubled down on his opposition to the idea of foreign peace-keeping troops being stationed in Ukraine if an agreement is reached, telling Witkoff and Kushner it would be considered by Russia as a "continuation of war."Fully integrating European representatives into future negotiations could also prove challenging, despite Witkoff's confidence on the matter. Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, who led Russia's delegation in Abu Dhabi, previously expressed skepticism over any European involvement.Yuri ⁠Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy adviser,​ told reporters ⁠after the Moscow meeting that the Russian President will continue talks on Ukraine with Trump ‌at the Asian-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in ‌China later this month.Despite the major obstacles that remain, Trump has expressed renewed optimism about ending the war—a goal he had previously claimed would be achieved on his first day back in office in 2025. “We're seeing a very strong inclination to end [the war between] Russia and Ukraine,” the President insisted during a press conference Monday.E.U. to present new Russia sanctions packageThe European Union is preparing a new sanctions package against Russia in an effort to increase economic pressure on Moscow and strengthen Ukraine's position in future peace talks.European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc was preparing its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, alongside a separate proposal to address Ukraine's financial needs, by the year-end.“We are, as a Commission, preparing a proposal [on] how to cover the financial needs of Ukraine in 2027, we will come with the sanctions package and the proposal for the financial needs before the next European Council,” she told reporters in Dublin. “We will support Ukraine, be it at wartime, or be it at peacetime."The next European Council meeting is scheduled to take place in Brussels across Nov. 26-27.Other European leaders also took the opportunity to underscore the importance of bolstering Ukraine.French President Emmanuel Macron said that “without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine,” insisting “there is no more U.S. support.”In an address at the summit, Zelensky appealed to Europe to continue supporting Ukrainian territory and championed sanctions against Russia as an effective measure.In a separate display of solidarity, the U.K. government announced new levies targeting Russia's 10 largest oil producers. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham described the move as “a sweep of stinging new sanctions to turn the screws on Russia’s oil revenues and drive forward an end to the Kremlin’s needless war.”Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, and Antonio Costa, president of the European Council, stand alongside Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and French President Emmanuel Macron at the European Political Community summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Nov. 12, 2026. —Brian Lawless—Getty ImagesZelensky says Starshield service is once again restrictedAs Witkoff and Kushner were meeting Russian officials in Moscow, Zelensky raised concerns about new speed restrictions on Starshield, the military-grade sister version of Elon Musk’s Starlink service.Zelensky said the Ukrainian military was facing "systematic" restrictions to Starshield and, as a result, struggling to intercept Russian drones. "This is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine," he said. "We are trying to clear up all circumstances with the American side."TIME has reached out to the White House and SpaceX for comment.Starlink offers Internet connectivity from satellites in low-Earth orbit. Its sister service Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon, relies on the Starlink network and has become a vital component for Ukrainian forces, strengthening its far-reaching drone strike missions and air defenses.Last month, Ukraine complained that speed restrictions had been imposed on Starshield, leading to the “failure” of several military missions. There were conflicting reports as to how the service came to be restricted.Reuters, citing three U.S. officials, had reported that the decision to limit the service came from inside the White House.When approached for comment, a senior U.S. official told TIME: “No such request was ever made by the President.”When initially addressing the matter, SpaceX founder and CEO Musk emphasized how Starlink and Starshield are different. He cited the U.S. authorities as being in control of the latter’s usage determinations.“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS,” he said on X. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”Musk later said his company SpaceX had imposed limits on the use of its Starlink satellite system, accusing Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity. He denied being behind the simultaneous issue with Starshield.Kyiv denied breaching Starlink’s terms of service. “It’s very strange that Elon Musk doesn’t know about the restrictions on Starlink in Ukraine,” said Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov via Telegram. “Starlink does not work over Russian territory. So we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and mid-range strikes.”
